title: Ariana Afghan Airlines 701
summary: A Boeing 727 en route from Kabul to London Gatwick descended below its correct glide slope in heavy freezing fog while approaching Gatwick Airport. The aircraft struck trees and houses near Fernhill, approximately 1.5 miles short of the runway, killing 50 people including 48 passengers and crew and two residents of a demolished house. The aircraft struck the ground 2000 meters from the runway beginning and rolled to the right.
probable_cause: The accident was primarily attributed to pilot error, specifically the failure to extend the flaps to maintain flight at the final approach speed. The heavy freezing fog restricted visual references during the critical approach phase.

The aircraft could not recover from the descent and struck terrain.

title: Viasa 742
summary: Viasa Flight 742, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9-32 registered YV-C-AVD, was on the Maracaibo-to-Miami leg of a flight from Caracas when it began its takeoff roll at 12:00 on 16 March 1969. Heading toward the Ziruma district, the aircraft failed to gain altitude and its left engine struck a power pole; as the plane banked left a reflector struck the fuel tank, spilling fuel, and after hitting a second power pole the left wing was ripped off and the left engine exploded into flames before the plane crashed in La Trinidad, Maracaibo. All 84 people aboard and 71 more on the ground were killed. Investigators attributed the crash to faulty sensors along with runway and takeoff calculations made from erroneous information, which left the aircraft overloaded by more than 5,000 pounds for the prevailing conditions.

title: 1969 Aswan Ilyushin Il-18 crash
summary: An Ilyushin Il-18 operated by United Arab Airlines, carrying Hajj pilgrims from Jeddah to Aswan, made two unsuccessful landing attempts in darkness with visibility reduced to 2-3 kilometers by a sandstorm on 20 March 1969. title: TWA 5787
summary: Trans World Airlines Flight 5787, a Boeing 707 on a non-revenue proficiency training flight, crashed at Atlantic City on July 26, 1969, killing all five crew on board. The aircraft was conducting recurrent training and proficiency checks including simulated single-engine failure during takeoff and landing. After landing on runway 13, the crew requested immediate turnaround and go-around on runway 31. During the go-around briefed as a three-engine ILS approach with simulated engine 4 failure, the flight engineer called for flaps 25 and gear up at decision height. However, neither flaps nor landing gear moved. Approximately 16-18 seconds after the go-around call, the crew commented that all hydraulic power had been lost due to fatigue failure in the left outboard spoiler actuator. With low airspeed, three engines, and no hydraulics for rudder control, directional control was lost, the aircraft rolled and pitched down, and impacted the ground.
probable_cause: Loss of hydraulic power to the rudder in a critical flight condition combined with poor procedures for simulating engine failures and failure to apply correct hydraulic loss procedures; loss of directional control was unrecoverable.

title: Allegheny Airlines 853
summary: Allegheny Airlines Flight 853, a McDonnell Douglas DC-9, collided mid-air with a privately owned Piper PA-28 near Fairland, Indiana, on September 9, 1969. The DC-9 was on an instrument flight plan descending for approach to Indianapolis at 3,550 feet when it converged with the VFR Piper aircraft at a relative speed of 350 mph. The left wing of the PA-28 sheared off the DC-9's rear tail assembly. Both aircraft lost control and crashed, killing all 83 occupants on both aircraft. The collision resulted from deficiencies in air traffic control radar capabilities, the see-and-avoid concept under mixed IFR/VFR conditions, and the absence of regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic in terminal areas.
probable_cause: The deficiencies in the collision avoidance capability of the Air Traffic Control system in a terminal area with mixed IFR and VFR traffic. The deficiencies included inadequacy of the see-and-avoid concept, technical limitations of radar in detecting all aircraft, and absence of Federal Aviation Regulations providing adequate separation of mixed traffic.

The FAA system lacked adequate regulations for separating mixed IFR and VFR traffic in terminal areas.
The report faulted military and civilian aviation authorities for not reducing well-known collision risks that had existed for over a year.

title: Mexicana de Aviación 801

title: Mohawk Airlines 411
summary: Mohawk Airlines Flight 411, a Fairchild Hiller FH-227 turboprop, departed Albany at 20:03 EST bound for Glens Falls with 11 passengers and 3 crew. At 20:20 EST, while executing a VOR approach, the aircraft hit trees on the northwest slope of Pilot Knob Mountain at low altitude, impacted a rock cliff, and fell 34 feet before becoming lodged in trees and catching fire. The NTSB concluded the crew executed an improper instrument approach using an unauthorized modified VOR/DME procedure instead of the only legally available VOR 1 approach, combined with a severe downdraft.
probable_cause: The captain's improper execution of an instrument approach, combined with a severe downdraft at low altitude, resulted in uncontrolled descent into terrain.

title: Nigeria Airways 925
summary: On 20 November 1969, Nigeria Airways Flight 925, a Vickers VC10 from London to Lagos with stops in Rome and Kano, crashed during final approach to Lagos International Airport. With landing gear down and flaps partially extended, the aircraft struck trees 13 kilometers short of runway 19 and crashed in thick forest. All 87 people on board were killed. The cause was not determined with certainty, but the flight recorder was not working, and investigators concluded it was most probably due to the crew being unaware of actual altitude during final approach.
probable_cause: Most probably the flight crew were unaware of the aircraft's actual altitude during the final approach and allowed the aircraft to come below safe height when not in visual contact with the ground. Fatigue may have also been a contributing factor.

title: Air France 212 (1969)
summary: Air France Flight 212, a Boeing 707 on the Caracas-to-Pointe-à-Pitre leg of a Santiago-to-Paris routing, took off from Caracas at 19:02 local time and about one minute later, at roughly 3,000 feet, plunged into the sea and sank in 160 feet of water, killing all 62 aboard. The BEA never published a report and the documents remain classified until 2029, so the cause was never established; theories include an evasive maneuver around a nearby Avro 748 followed by loss of control, a bomb, spatial disorientation, in-flight fire, engine failure and fuel contamination.

factors.evidence: maneuvers to avoid colliding with a nearby Avro 748 followed by a loss of control

the aircraft plunged into the sea and sank in 160 feet of water

events.text: The aircraft took off on the Caracas-Pointe-à-Pitre leg from runway 08R at 19:02 local time (23:02 UTC).
One minute after takeoff, at approximately 3,000 feet, the aircraft plunged into the sea and sank in 160 feet of water.
Theories about the crash have included a maneuver to avoid colliding with a nearby Avro 748 followed by loss of control, and a bomb-related explosion.

notes: BEA never published its report; cause unconfirmed among competing theories cited in the article.

title: Olympic Airways 954
summary: Olympic Airways Flight 954, a Douglas DC-6B on a domestic flight from Chania, Crete, to Athens, struck Mount Paneio near Keratea at approximately 2,000 feet with its undercarriage retracted while on approach to Athens on 8 December 1969. Rain and high winds prevailed at the time, and all 85 passengers and 5 crew aboard were killed. Investigators ruled that the flight crew had deviated from the proper track and descended below the minimum safe altitude while making an ILS approach.
